# Software modules (and why `module avail` lies) {#sec-modules}

::: {.tldr}
Software comes from **Lmod modules** you `module load`. The system is *hierarchical*: many
packages are invisible until you first load a compiler. So `module avail` only shows what's
reachable *right now* and will swear things don't exist — use **`module spider <name>`** to
find the truth and learn what to load first.
:::

## Why modules exist

A cluster has hundreds of users who need mutually incompatible software: three versions of
Python, five compilers, conflicting builds of GDAL. You can't install all of that globally.
Instead, **modules** let you load exactly the versions you want into *your* shell for *this*
session, without affecting anyone else. Load a module and its programs appear on your `PATH`;
unload it and they vanish.

```bash
module load gcc/14.2.0        # add gcc 14 to this shell
module list                   # what do I currently have loaded?
module unload gcc/14.2.0      # remove it
module purge                  # clear everything and start clean
```

## The hierarchy — the thing that confuses everyone

MedicineBow uses **Lmod** in *hierarchical* mode. Modules are arranged in layers:

- **Core** modules are always visible: the compilers (`gcc`, `nvhpc-sdk`, `oneapi`), MPI,
  and standalone tools.
- **Compiler-dependent** modules — Python, R, GDAL, NetCDF, HDF5, CUDA — are **hidden until
  you load a compiler.** They were built against a specific compiler, so Lmod won't show them
  until you've picked one.

This is why a brand-new user runs `module avail`, doesn't see `gdal`, and concludes it isn't
installed. It is — it's just one layer down.

::: {.callout-important}
## Use `module spider`, not `module avail`, to answer "does X exist?"
`module avail` shows only what's loadable *given what you've already loaded* — it lies by
omission. **`module spider`** searches the entire tree and tells you both that something
exists and what you must load first to reach it.

```bash
module spider gdal            # yes it exists; here are the versions
module spider gdal/3.13.0     # ...and exactly what to load before it
```
:::

A typical geospatial stack, in order:

```bash
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0        # 1. a compiler, first
module load gdal/3.13.0       # 2. now GDAL is reachable
module load netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi
```

## What's installed (a tour)

Ask the machine for the current list with `module spider`, but roughly:

- **Compilers (core):** `gcc/{11.4.0, 11.5.0, 13.2.0, 14.2.0, 15.2.0}`, `nvhpc-sdk`,
  `oneapi`, `openmpi/5.0.10`.
- **After loading a compiler:** `python/{3.10.6, 3.12.0, 3.14.4}`, `r/{4.4.0, 4.5.3}`,
  `gdal/{3.7.3, 3.13.0}`, `netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi`, `hdf5/1.14.3*`,
  `cuda-toolkit/{12.4.1, 12.6.1}`, `openmpi/4.1.6`, `rclone/1.63.1`.
- **Standalone:** `apptainer/{1.3.5, 1.4.1}`, `singularity/4.1.0`, `miniconda3/24.3.0`,
  `julia/{1.10.3, 1.11.6}`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The GPU compiler contradiction
`gcc/13.2.0` prints a deprecation warning telling you to move to `gcc/14.2.0`. But
`cuda-toolkit` is **only built against `gcc/13.2.0`**. So GPU users have to knowingly load
the "deprecated" compiler:

```bash
module load gcc/13.2.0        # yes, the one that warns you — CUDA needs it
module load cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
```

Ignore the warning in this case; it's a packaging quirk, not a mistake on your part.
:::

## Making a set of modules load automatically

Once you know the stack a project needs, save it as a named collection so you don't retype it:

```bash
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 gdal/3.13.0 netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi
module save firestack          # remember this set as "firestack"

# next session:
module restore firestack
```

Prefer `module restore` in your submit scripts over hand-loading a long list — it's
reproducible and self-documents the environment your job needs.

::: {.callout-note}
## Load modules *in your submit script*, not just interactively
The modules you load on the login node don't automatically carry into a batch job the way
you'd expect across a fresh environment. Put the `module load` / `module restore` lines
**inside** your `sbatch` script so the job builds the same environment every time
(@sec-anatomy).
:::

When a package isn't available as a module — or you need a pip/conda world — that's the next
chapter (@sec-conda).
